intro_html: One piece, seven moves, always in this order. The rice stays airy in the middle and firmer at the edge: a dimple traps the air, and the later locks only firm the sides. Written for a right-handed cook. The left hand holds the fish and the piece. The right hand brings the rice and does the locks and the press. The flip in this sequence is kote-gaeshi — forward over the left fingertips, so the fish ends on top. Start with sushi rice at about body temperature, and practise a few rice-only pieces before you use fish.

notes.html:
• Each shaping picture is painted over a 3D model of the two hands, posed joint by joint for that move, so every finger sits where the step text puts it.
  • The close-ups show the same pose from another angle.

• A short shaping list often says “flip it using one of the four styles” and then continues with a side lock, a top press, a half-turn and a second seal.
  • That lock only makes sense once the fish is already up, so the flip has to land the fish on top.
  • Kote-gaeshi is that flip: forward over the fingertips, around the long side.
  • Tate-gaeshi and hon-te-gaeshi are other turns, used for toppings that slide or in a few older shops.
  • Itte-gaeshi and yokote-gaeshi are names with no published step-by-step, so drawing them would be a guess.
  • This page teaches the seven moves, and only kote-gaeshi.

• Side lock: right thumb and middle finger, index lifted (Ginza Watari, Tencho, Sushi University).
  • Some shops use the index and thumb instead (Niizu), or the left thumb as well (Yoshino-zushi).
  • Top press: the right index pushes down a little into the cupped left hand.
  • Several sources instead rest the right fingers on top and lift the left hand into them; that seats the fish less clearly, so it is not the move here.
  • Roll direction: forward, away from you, over the fingertips.
  • One source says toward you.
  • The axis — around the long side — is the usual reading; no source states it in so many words.

• Don't flatten and smear the rice with the thumb before the dimple, and don't square the short ends while the fish is still underneath.
  • Both pack the center or pre-shape a rectangle the later locks are meant to make.
  • The only touch on the rice before the flip is the center dimple.
notes.title_html: What not to do before the flip

notes.html:
• About 18–20 g of rice per piece (15 g for a small one).
  • Before the Taisho era pieces were 2–4 times this size.

• Airy center, firm edge.
  • The dimple is the air; the two side locks are the edge.
  • Few movements, light pressure: the rice should hold on the way to the soy and come apart in the mouth.
  • Every extra press packs it denser.

• Swap every hand: fish and piece in the right hand, rice and pressing with the left.
  • The half-turn goes counter-clockwise.

• Buy fish sold for raw eating and keep it cold until you slice it.
  • Salmon for sushi should have been frozen first.
  • Eat nigiri the day it's made.

steps.body_html:
• Mix the cold water and rice vinegar in a small bowl.
  • Dip the right middle finger to the first joint and rub the water over both palms.
  • Clap off the excess — one hand a loose fist, one open. Damp, not wet: too much water and the rice falls apart.

how.caption: Middle finger into the tezu, to the first joint.
Rub it over both palms, then clap off the excess.

steps.title: Tezu: wet the hands

steps.body_html:
• Cut across the grain (the faint white lines).
  • Tilt the knife 30–45°, set the heel on the far edge and draw it towards you in one long pull — don't saw.
  • Slices about 7–8 cm long, 3 cm wide and 3–5 mm thick, about 14 g each.

how.caption: One long pull towards you, knife tilted 30–45°.

steps.title: Slice the fish

uses_rows.amount_html: ~200 g (16 slices)
uses_rows.name_html: Sashimi-grade tuna or salmon, a block (saku)

steps.body_html:
• Left hand palm up. Lay the slice on the inner side of the left index, middle and ring fingers. Its long side runs parallel to the knuckles, and it sits on the finger roots — the crease where those fingers meet the palm — not in the hollow of the palm and not out on the fingertips. Cut face down, against the skin. The little finger lies alongside and steadies the end of the fish.
  • The right index fingertip, the pad with the nail facing up, sets a pea of wasabi in the center of the fish.
  • The right thumb, index and middle fingertips cage 18–20 g of rice into a loose oblong. Do not squeeze. A tight ball has no air left for the dimple, and it cracks when the sides are locked later.
  • Set that oblong on the wasabi, long side matching the fish. Bend the left fingers a little at the middle knuckles, which sit just past the far side of the piece, so the fish rises into a shallow cusp under the rice. The fingertips rise beside the piece; they don't curl over the rice.

steps.title: Form and cusp

uses_rows.amount_html: ~300 g (18–20 g each)

steps.body_html:
• Take the right hand fully off the piece.
  • Bend the left thumb and press the pad — not the nail — straight down into the exact center of the rice, halfway between the two ends, not along a side. The hollow is about the width of the thumb tip, and the tip sinks about 0.5 cm — a quarter of the rice's height. Rice stays visible all around the thumb.
  • The other left fingers stay underneath and do not squeeze. Don't smear the rice toward the ends: spreading it packs the center this dimple is there to keep open.

steps.title: The indentation

steps.body_html:
• This sequence uses kote-gaeshi. The piece is still fish down, rice up. Keep the base knuckles flat (they may tip back a little) and curl the middle and end joints of the left index, middle and ring fingers up around the far long edge of the rice, pads near its top corner. Those three fingertip pads are the only contact on that edge.
  • Straighten those three fingers together. The piece rolls forward over the fingertips, around its long side, staying on the pads the whole way, and lands fish up on the left fingers.
  • The right index pad and the right thumb pad catch the two long flanks — not the short ends — and slide the piece back into the same crease at the finger roots. The thumb only holds; the index pushes. The right middle finger stays off for this move.
  • Other turns exist — tate-gaeshi, hon-te-gaeshi — and two further names have no published step-by-step. They are not this sequence, so they are not drawn here.

steps.title: The flip

steps.body_html:
• Fish is up. The right hand comes in from your side, palm down, fingers pointing away from you. The right thumb pad presses the near long flank, midway along it, halfway up the rice, below the fish. Not on a short end.
  • The right middle finger — the longest finger — bends so its pad presses the far long flank, opposite the thumb. The squeeze is sideways, inward, until those two edges are straight.
  • The right index finger stays lifted: straight, pointing away from you and a little up, its tip the highest point of that hand, a clear gap between it and the fish. It does not touch the piece. The right ring and little fingers stay curled into the palm.
  • The left hand only cradles: fingers in a shallow cup, left thumb off to the side, not pinching an end. Don't crush the center: the dimple is still the air inside.

steps.title: Side lock

steps.body_html:
• The right index fingertip — the pad of that one finger, nail up — taps the center of the fish and presses it lightly down into the curl of the left hand. The left fingers stay bent at the middle knuckles, so the piece sits in the cup.
  • The left fingers stay curled. This is one finger pressing, not two fingers resting on top like a lid.
  • Light pressure. The right thumb and the other three right fingers stay clear, with a visible gap. You are seating the fish, not packing the rice.

steps.title: Top press

steps.body_html:
• Turn it end for end in two quarter turns, clockwise as you look down. One hand can't turn a pinched piece the whole 180° — the elbow would have to swing behind the piece.
  • First quarter: bring the right hand in from the right, fingers pointing left. The right thumb pad takes the near long side, the right index pad the far long side, midway. Lift about 1 cm, turn a quarter clockwise — the fingers end up pointing away from you — and set it down.
  • Second quarter: let go, bring the hand back in from the right, fingers pointing left, the hand above the piece. The thumb pad takes the right long side, the one nearest your hand; the index pad reaches over the top to the left long side. Lift, turn the second quarter, set it down.
  • It goes back into the same crease at the base of the left fingers, not the middle of the palm and not the fingertips. The end that was toward the index finger is now toward the little finger.

steps.title: The 180° rotate

steps.body_html:
• Side lock again: the right thumb pad and the right middle-finger pad on the long flanks, index lifted and not touching.
  • Top press again: the right index fingertip, the pad only, light, into the curl of the left hand.
  • That is the seal. Don't add another wrap around the middle — every extra press packs the rice.
  • From the side it looks like a boat: fish draped over the top, bottom rounded.

steps.title: Final seal

steps.body_html:
• Fish draped over the top with a little overhang, a rounded boat-shaped bottom, one bite.
  • Serve straight away with soy sauce and ginger. Dip the fish side, not the rice.
steps.title: Serve

timeline.note_html: Slice the fish in small batches and keep the rest of the block covered in the fridge. Work fast: warm hands warm the fish, and every extra movement packs the rice.
